newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Rain drenches Britain's end-of-empire farewell.
newsitem.headline: Rain drenches Britain's end-of-empire farewell.

text.p: It rained on the last parade of the British empire on Monday.
The European island synonymous with soggy weather retreated from its last major imperial outpost under a drenching downpour.
But true to tradition, the marching bands and skirling pipers bravely put on their last great show east of Suez with an open-air concert at the Hong Kong harbour.
Britons held their heads high under 1997 commemorative umbrellas as troops marched, singers serenaded, dancers pranced and sparkling dragons snaked as the sun set.

Ten thousand people packed a stadium on the seafront where the British royal yacht Britannia and warship HMS Chatham were moored, ready to sail away after Queen Elizabeth's son Prince Charles handed Hong Kong to China's President Jiang Zemin.
The sea of umbrellas in the Hong Kong setting resembled people wearing giant coolie hats.
Midway through the three-hour ceremony the rain stopped and spirits lifted among the crowd of mainly British residents. But then it started again.
Hong Kong's 28th and last governor, Chris Patten, rain running down his suit, fought to hold back the tears after receiving an ovation for his farewell speech.
He declared Hong Kong's unshakeable destiny was that its own people would run its affairs. No dependent territory had ever achieved more prosperity, he said.
He wished Hong Kong well in "the challenging years ahead" as an autonomous Special Administrative Region of China.
Then he sat down and bowed his head, biting back tears as the crowd roared.

He had to stand and wave in acknowledgement before they quietened and a band struck up with the music of Edward Elgar, whose works are often held to reflect an Edwardian era's sense of personal loss and imperial transience.
